messages.subject: dplyr for an ODBC source
parts:
Hello, I'm trying to bend RODBCDBI and dplyr to work on an ODBC data source, and there's a few changes needed in different places. 

The key ones I need are for dplyr: 

1) I need to quote columns and table names with square brackets, so I write my own sql_escape_string() and sql_escape_ident() methods with a paste0("[", x, "]") step, which seems fine. 

2) Harder is the LIMIT clause which is not supported by my DB, the equivalent to this is the TOP clause that comes before column names. (This is where I get to the "I’d strongly recommend asking for help" part of Adding  a new SQL backend. :)

So where the standard seems to be
SELECT  "ID" "X",
FROM "Table"
LIMIT 10

I need this

SELECT TOP 10 [ID], [X],
FROM [Table]

I'm trying to do this for Manifold GIS, which has system-installed ODBC data sources - the SQL dialect is closer to Access and SQL Server, but I don't know the details of that. I don't know how widely applicable what I'm trying will be for ODBC, but I'm very keen to get this working at all. 

I will put together my other changes for RODBCDBI as a pull request, though I'm still learning how to write the underlying methods properly.  

I'll be happy to explore the use of this for other sources like Excel, Access, SQL Server and so on. 

Cheers, MIke. 
--

messages.author: d66aa3feb509150a
messages.subject: Re: dplyr for an ODBC source
parts:
Ok, I got this work by writing my own sql_select.ODBCConnection. 

This is it: 

sql_select.ODBCConnection <- 
function (con, select, from, where = NULL, group_by = NULL, having = NULL, 
    order_by = NULL, limit = NULL, offset = NULL, ...) 
{
    out <- vector("list", 8)
    names(out) <- c("select", "from", "where", "group_by", "having", 
        "order_by", "limit", "offset")
    assertthat::assert_that(is.character(select), length(select) > 0L)
    
   
        if (!is.null(limit)) {
          assertthat::assert_that(is.integer(limit), length(limit) == 1L)
          ## TOP clause is part of SELECT
           out$select <- build_sql("SELECT ", " TOP ", limit, " ",  escape(select, collapse = ", ", 
        con = con))
        } else {
    
      out$select <- build_sql("SELECT", escape(select, collapse = ", ", 
        con = con))
        }
    
    assertthat::assert_that(is.character(from), length(from) == 1L)
    out$from <- build_sql("FROM ", from, con = con)
    if (length(where) > 0L) {
        assertthat::assert_that(is.character(where))
        out$where <- build_sql("WHERE ", escape(where, collapse = " AND ", 
            con = con))
    }
    if (!is.null(group_by)) {
        assertthat::assert_that(is.character(group_by), length(group_by) > 
            0L)
        out$group_by <- build_sql("GROUP BY ", escape(group_by, 
            collapse = ", ", con = con))
    }
    if (!is.null(having)) {
        assertthat::assert_that(is.character(having), length(having) == 1L)
        out$having <- build_sql("HAVING ", escape(having, collapse = ", ", 
            con = con))
    }
    if (!is.null(order_by)) {
        assertthat::assert_that(is.character(order_by), length(order_by) > 
            0L)
        out$order_by <- build_sql("ORDER BY ", escape(order_by, 
            collapse = ", ", con = con))
    }

    if (!is.null(offset)) {
        assertthat::assert_that(is.integer(offset), length(offset) == 1L)
        out$offset <- build_sql("OFFSET ", offset, con = con)
    }
    escape(unname(dplyr:::compact(out)), collapse = "\n", parens = FALSE, 
        con = con)
}


Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: dplyr for an ODBC source
parts:
Just to kill this off, I've put partly working examples here, with both Manifold GIS and Access: 

https://github.com/mdsumner/dplyrodbc

With Manifold I've wrapped it so you can point to any project file, no need for a DSN. 

There's a long way to go but it's looking promising!

Also, I consider this a throwaway "dply-odbc" package, it's probably best used as more atomic pieces for specific applications. It's pretty straightforward to modify the classes and methods as needed. 

Thanks again.
